comments.name: Name
comments.body:
A solid argument can be made that our modern economic structure is not capitalism, at least not according to the definition first set forth by Adam Smith. Theories developed from economic structures so fundamentally different from our own are unhelpful for identifying solutions to the problems we confront.

Consider, for example, the concept of labor power. Whether from a farming the land subsistence or excess to basic needs hourly wage perspective, the average person within the modern economy does not have the power to ensure they receive the equivalent of basic subsistence (housing, food, water, clothing, and access to the tech essentials necessary to access our society and economy) through death. We lost access to the theoretical commons and its ability to enable us to create our own means for subsistence. We lost access to subsequent exchange of labor power for wage dependency enabling subsistence plus an excess we could bargain over. 

The "affordability" problem is more aptly described as a structural subsistence problem. In the public and private sectors, most people are dependent upon below subsistence wages. And that is before considering the definitions of productivity and value.

I don't have a solution. I have no hope helpful paths forward are available. But all potential solutions will remain impossible until and unless we honestly and correctly review and assess the current economic reality - and create descriptive definitions that fit reality, not fantasy.

I started quilting in my late 50's.  I learned from a group of hand quilters.  I have three hand-quilted queen bed sized quilts which I rotate annually on my bed.  Relatives got wedding, anniversary,and baby quilts.  Friends because I felt like it.  Foster kids one year got 11.  Meals on Wheels got over 300 placemats from our small quilt grip of six.   You do the math.

I always have a couple of charity quilts ready to go for the inevitable Colorado wildfire.  I had to quit hand quilting about 12 years ago due to arthritis in my thumbs so now machine and free motion quilt.  I have downsized and moved into art quilting.  I only have domestic machines, a small one for traveling and an old Singer which was a wedding present from my father-in-law who was an engineer at Singer.  It has metal gears, no belts, no computer boards to go out, and I maintain it myself as most repair shops won't touch it.  I have a PhD in chemistry and operated ma as spectrometers during my career, the first instruments similarly not computerized.

Sewing, gardening, baking sourdough and from scratch are all satisfying occupations which provide a state of flow during the creation and a product which is tangible and rewarding.

Your start-up execs commit the cardinal sin besetting all of Techdom - they mistake statistics for reality.

One edges always towards "truth".  The other is a pure creation of men... men with their pride, their interests, their needs and goals, prejudices and preferences.

Statistics would be the second one, for those left wondering.

Like America's Constitution outside the crust-laden halls of SCOTUS, statistics is alive and wiggling.  Constantly refined and reinterpreted, improved and argued over.

Their interviews and games are proxies, meant to represent something they can never fairly represent or, as in this case, choose not to.  In this context they are no gift to mankind, or to candidates, as you report here.

These Bros deceive themselves and expect Hosannahs in return.

On the other hand, what up with "candidates"?

They want to start work, sign up with companies and corporations already having abandoned almost a million employees because the "gift" of AI renders them useless, wasteful. in corporate terms "superfluous"?

I get it... somebody has to buy lunch, even if its only for a little while.

Well... no.

Hiring is done by the risk-averse. If they go by what the computer or algorithm tells them is a good candidate, they can blame the program if it's a fail. If they hire someone who already has done that job for 5 years, and it's a fail, they can blame the previous employer and pat themselves on the back for having better employees. If they hire from a top school, they went to the best, and the best failed, not them.

If they hire someone on their network of connections, there's a payback lurking out there, waiting to be cashed in.

But if they take a chance, on a lower grade, or less experience, or a less well known program, they own any failure.

The fact that they'd own any success is not relevant.

comments.name: Pat Shediack
comments.body:
I retired in December 2022 after 46 years of work with 44 of that as a supervisor of some kind or another and 39 as a project manager in various business, technical or government areas.  I also earned my master of science in management specializing in project management as well as the global PM certification.  Three years into retirement, I'm still receiving inquiries from companies about interviewing with them.  

When I read the job descriptions I'm sent I see a grocery list of requirements that literally no one I ever encountered in the PM field could meet--including me.  It's pretty obvious the job requirements are nothing more than a hiring manager's list of "I wants", "I'd like" and "It would be great if we could get someone who also do X, Y or Z".  HR then plugged into various data entry fields in their AI-based recruiting system which screened the incoming resumes.  In short, the company is looking for a unicorn.    

If hiring managers are looking for "unicorns", they're on a fool's mission.  The HR managers and staff helping them search for those "unicorns" are just as foolish.  

For those job seekers who can't seem to break through the AI resume screening system, try some other things like joining whatever professional society, trade group or business group relates to your field, go in the military or apply for public service or non-profit jobs.  Make a grocery list of every single skill you have, then apply to global, national & local firms who use those skills.

The number of applications for a single position was staggering (this is back in the early to mid-2010's) and most of the applicants were completely unqualified, and I mean they had absolutely no business applying for the job.  The HR representative was using some sort of screening tool just to make the task manageable.  Then I would pick up and start screening the rest.  It was still a daunting task and the candidates were underwhelming.  In another more recent situation, again hiring a leader of a small organization, the number of applicants was very high and the quality of the those at the top was not as high as I would expect.  Again, many of the applicants had absolutely no business applying for the job, meaning that their own description of their skill set didn't remotely match the job description.

comments.name: NY Times Reader
comments.body:
I seem to recall the late Spring 1982 / June 1982 as being extremely difficult, and likely more so than now.....why?...16% prime interest rate, inflation over 6% and of course there were were no cell phones, no smart phones, no computers, no internet and no one was hiring because national unemployment was 9.5%.....I bought dimes by the roll to used them in pay phones to reach HR people, hiring managers and anyone who I could get on the phone for any position on Wall Street...and it worked!!...how else could one get a job back in those days? More education (beyond 4 years) and more debt was not the answer (not for me, anyway) and may not be now, too.

My advice to graduates, take nothing for granted, get that first job through sheer effort of job applications, making human connections where possible, diligent follow-up, make spreadsheets of who you have contacted and who to contact next...you'll succeed but sadly, for now, it will be a job in and of itself...do not stop trying!.

comments.name: AhBrightWings
comments.body:
While no movie can ever encapsulate a work of such vast complexity and nuance, Nolan achieves something monumental. He dispenses with entire episodes (Nausikaa), collapses others into one, and glosses over or erases entire scenes, but in remaining true to his own vision, he does Homer full justice.  I loved how he kept returning to the Trojan War as an instigating and destructive force. 

A few quibbles that don't feel minor:

If you include the Polyphemus/Cyclops episode, as you must, why drop the most spectacular part of it—the “Nobody” trick? The Greeks saw it as Odysseus’s greatest stratagem after the Trojan horse. It captures his fatal complexity perfectly: clever enough to tell Polyphemus his name is “Nobody,” which saves the crew when the Cyclops cries that “Nobody” is hurting him, yet arrogant enough, once safely at sea, to taunt him and announce his real name, lineage, and kingdom. That single burst of hubris is what dooms them; it is the moment Poseidon turns against Odysseus.

Why leave out the harrowing moment when Helen walks past the Trojan horse, hears the men whispering inside, and faces an impossible choice? She can betray Odysseus's men or save them by keeping their secret and, in doing so, betray her adopted country of Troy. She chooses the latter, leaving her with as much blood on her hands as Odysseus. She puns that she calls Troy "Destroy."

Despite those misses, Nolan’s own vision is cohesive, compelling, and devastating. He's reanimated a lost world.

This is the exact situation that my parents experienced long ago: they bought their first house from the original builder, but couldn't get the existing tenants to move out.  They had 2 young kids and one on the way. 

They went to court in the summer and it took months to gain possession.  We moved in on Dec. 24th 1945 so I've been told, and my father had to kick in a basement window to gain entry.  

I was 2½ years old; my sister was 4.  The house was a 1½ storey brick place that cost my folks $35. a month for 8 years and 4 months, paid in cash to Mr. Reuben Jackson, the builder.

I sold my mother's house on Long Island in 2020. The buyer was a builder. We arranged for her to stay a month or two after the title closing. Attorneys papered the sale and the stay terms. The builder was smart. He paid about 80% ($1.5 million) at closing and held back about $200k to be paid upon Mom's vacating premises. Obviously my 83 year old mother was not going to squat her former, old home after receiving the big lump sum and having a six figure receivable on the hook. 

As it concerns having a key that is not an issue to argue. All landlords have keys to their properties. They simply must follow tenant law as to access.

comments.name: Ready to ROC
comments.body: We sold a house recently and stayed in it for 6 weeks after the sale.  However, everything about our tenancy was negotiated as part of the sales agreement.  We wanted that as much as the buyer did.  Being a landlord, or tenant, with no contractual agreement as to each parties duties and responsibilities isn't sound business or real estate practice.  Every thing worked out in our post-sale possession for us and the buyer, but a negotiated rental agreement is essential to increase the potential for that outcome.  Closing in this situation and hoping for the best can lead to some very difficult, and expensive to remediate, consequences.

comments.name: Alicia Walker
comments.body:
We bought our home in December '99. The sellers were building their dream home in Orange County. They wanted to rent back to us for 6 mos while their home was being built.  We were first time home buyers and were living in an apartment we loved. We were bidding against a family that had a larger down payment than we did. My husband calculated the rent  they would charge the seller for the competing family.  
We offered them a lower rent than the other family and they took our bid even though our down payment was smaller. (But the price they were selling it for was the same for both parties) We had a well written contract and everything went pretty smoothly. But there is no way I would rent back without a valid contract.  We assumed they would be keeping their gardeners.  They didn't and the yard was very overgrown.  We would have happily paid for the gardener but they didn't even give us the opportunity to pay them.

comments.name: Stickyfingers
comments.body: A seller in Ohio had a similar request of me. The realtor tried to assure me this was normal and customary. In fact, a lot of the listing sheets said "Possession 30 (or more) days after closing." I assured her, "I'm not from these parts," and I do business differently. If the seller needs more time to move out, we can simply have a later closing date, I'm flexible. But the day of the closing, we do a walk through, I get the keys, and adios to the sellers. Some hurt feelings, but they came around.

comments.body: I moved to a small Mexican beach town full time 7 years ago, (after visiting for long stays in prior years) and have watched the rising tide of tourism floating in on larger and larger buses to see the one big landmark.  I’m hyper aware that I am an immigrant to this place and work hard to be a positive part of the local and cultural fabric of our Tiny Town.  When f&f visit, we gladly share our favorite spots because it helps those businesses but also include amongst that other experiential moments like volunteering at a spay&neuter clinic, donating to the local school art projects or participating in local language and cooking classes.   We can’t stop it but perhaps we can help re-direct it into a more positive result. Having said that I did have to ask a friend to remove  geo-tags from a post about a sweet secret beach we showed  them - because the landscape would not support such an influx on the daily. comments.body:
Years ago I lived in Hawaii and tourists would regularly ask me, sotto voce, where the 'secret' beaches were. I would look them in the eye and reply that if I told them, they wouldn't be secret, now would they? They were always kind of shocked.

It's worse now. I live in Africa, and we have a very large private wildlife reserve, which is unfenced so as not to impede natural wildlife migrations. We are regularly finding people 'wild camping' on the land, thanks to an app called iOverlander that posts fabulous spots to 'wild camp', AKA trespass, on private land.

I've contacted the app and demanded they remove the designations. I've rated it and complained to the App Store and will continue to do so.
Because of major wildfire and poaching problems, camping outside of designated areas is illegal in this country, and there are three commercial campsites within 10 kms of these illegal sites. It would cost tens of thousands of dollars to re-fence the land, money that currently goes to conservation projects. We will no longer be polite when asking people to pack up and leave. The entitlement of tourists is breathtaking.

The “gatekeepers” and activists so often only sit on a residency timeline slightly longer than the tourists themselves. I surmise it’s because unlike born-and-raised locals, they are often well-enough-off gentrifiers who can afford to live without tourists and want to keep their hotspots - typically operated by born-and-raised locals, who see the tourists as a boon - cheap and quiet for themselves.

It is certainly true in my own regional vacation destination - the schoolteachers who could afford waterfront homes have long since been driven away, replaced by second homeowners or well-off remote workers, retirees and artists who complain about the tourists. While the born-and-raised locals are barely clinging on and only then thanks to catering to tourists.

(I have to wonder if there was sexism involved as the idea of a woman writing a much tougher and more accurate story of life on the prairie might not have gone over well.) At the time the family really needed money and Laura went with the children's version. 

Much as I enjoyed the Little House books as a child, I really wish Laura had written the adult version. I think we lost a lot when she didn't. And the books she did write added to a highly romantized version of "going west" that continues to shape our nation's mythology today, sometimes in unfortunate ways and I'm not talking just about racism. For one thing, Pa Ingalls' restless insistence on pulling up stakes as soon as communities began to form in what used to be frontier made for a lot of adventure but also kept the family in poverty. It really does take a village, something we like to forget with the emphasis we place on rugged individualism.

The stadium is in Bergen County, NJ, where Spain and Argentina play for the trophy this afternoon. Bergen County also happens to enforce some of the strictest blue laws left in the U.S.: general merchandise sales are banned on Sundays. 

Bergen County has some of the largest retail complexes in the country, magnets for exactly the kind of international tourist traffic a World Cup Final brings, will have their clothing, electronics, and furniture sections effectively closed to shoppers, by state statute that dates to the 1950s.

So a Spanish fan wanting to buy a jersey after the match, or an Argentine visitor needing a jacket for the cold front behind those two goals, will discover that "sacred Sunday" isn't just a German constitutional quirk, it's also across the Hudson River from Times Square. Restaurants, bars, and the stadium concessions will be running at full tilt, of course; it's only retail that stops. Since open source models can be hosted by anyone, the market will drive down the cost of AI to marginal cost--which makes frontier AI a commodity. That is bad news for Silicon Valley, but in the long run, it is good news for the economy. It prevents Silicon Valley from charging high rents on their AI models and capturing for themselves the value of the productivity benefits that AI creates. That means that AI adoption will be accelerated and AI technology will diffuse faster to the overall economy than would otherwise be the case. And AI adoption and diffusion is the #1 driver of future productivity growth, which is essential to the health and wealth of the U.S economy. Therefore, the Chinese are really doing us a favor. The growing frustration with public officials leveraging their office for personal or political gain points to a deeper, structural failure. The presidential pardon.(Article II, Section 2), is functionally absolute and a relic modeled after the British "royal prerogative of mercy." Hamilton argued that a single executive needed this power for swift execution during national crises. Instead, it has evolved into a tool for political cronyism and self-preservation, completely unchecked by Congress or the judiciary.

A rational system would treat this power as a high-stakes legal exception, perhaps requiring a unanimous Supreme Court recommendation or explicit legislative approval before a pardon is finalized. By making the amendment process practically impossible in a polarized era, we have frozen the rules of the game in 1787. Jayson Conner(48) and Jeffrey Newman (58)
An extraordinary couple whose nonprofit program Backpacks for the Streets has donated and distributed more than 180,000 backpacks fully loaded with daily essentials to those who live on the streets of New York.  
Mr. Conner and Mr. Newman died within days of each other.

Since 2018, they and their dozens of volunteers have provided a vital network of support to those they serve.
All year round.
All year strong.
Giving away the backpacks was initially a side project of their nonprofit, Together Helping Others, which provided a range of social services throughout the area where they discovered that unhoused people often lacked something as simple as a container to hold their belongings. What people in that situation needed, the two men figured, was sturdy backpacks.
	
“Everything about the backpack is about hope,” Mr. Newman told Fox News in 2020. “We understand that it’s not going to cure homelessness; we don’t pretend it’s going to cure homelessness. But it does say to somebody, ‘Hey, you know what? We care.’”

In addition to requesting monetary donations, they listed specific supplies that people could donate on the organization’s Amazon wish list.

Mr. Newman told ABC News in 2020. “We’re not making little goody bags — we’re really thinking out what it is that people need the most.  It's a labor of love"
	
May their memories be a blessing.

"On the Radio"

Lorain, Ohio, was an International City. Immigrants flocked to U.S. Steel, Ford, American Shipbuilding, Fruehauf. Cranes emblazoned with the name LORAIN came from Thew Shovel.

We were taught Lorain had the largest population of Puerto Ricans outside of Puerto Rico and NYC.

Each nationality had its own enclave. Its own churches (and synagogues), its own bars.

Unity came when New Restaurants arrived. A sit-down pizza place (not just takeout or cafeteria pizza at the high school). 1st Chinese restaurant: the Golden Dragon. Each addition was another rung up the ladder of Sophistication.

Restaurants broadened my palate. But it was radio that expanded my mind.

A cheap yellow transistor radio. WABC & WMCA out of NYC, if late-night cloud cover allowed for it. WCFL/WLS from Chicago. Windsor-Detroit's CKLW (before Canadian Content). WIXY from nearby Cleveland.

Distant places. But it wasn't the distance that changed me. It was the lyrics.

The 1st song I ever wrote down the lyrics to: Janis Ian's "Society's Child." A taboo interracial romance ending badly. Every 3 hours, I jotted down a line.

"Abraham, Martin and John." "Ohio." (One of the 4 killed at Kent State was from Lorain.) "Get Together." "Everyday People." "War."

"Imagine."

I became an Idealist late night on AM radio. A revolutionary in my heart.

Which is why, these days, I find it hard to listen to radio -- FM or AM. Such chaos in the world. So much division. Where is our "Imagine"?

Hugs,
Phil G

Sibling relationships are more unique and varied than any other. Unlike parental or spousal relationships, you can be best friends or you can be totally estranged and society won't bat an eye. Sibling relationships come in as many flavors as cat personalities.

A failed spousal or partner relationship often ends with estrangement and replacement; the ex becomes ancient history from a relatively short time long ago. Parents lose their potency over your sense of self as you get older, and at advanced ages the roles can become confusing reversed.
 
Not so with siblings. I see a world of possibilities realized among friends and family: some siblings talk on the phone even every day and take vacations together. Others are totally estranged. A majority fall somewhere in the middle, together for holidays or major events for the nieces and nephews, but with only occasional and irregular contact.

That such "horizontal" relationships can be deemed secondary in the world of therapy and psychiatry surprises me. It's fertile ground.

If this comment strikes you as coming from a younger brother who would have liked this kind of exploration with his late older sibling, bingo.

As someone with a zoonotic disease focus I really want folks to understand that the most efficient way to control mosquito populations, and the vector-borne diseases they carry, is the way nature intended - mosquito predators.
And bats are the best at catching them - one bat might consume on average 1000-3000 mosquitoes per night, the little brown bat even up to 1200 every hour.
Welcome every bat you see, it may just save your life, if it catches the exact mosquito that would have infected you with a vector-borne disease that would have made you really, really sick...
For me, every bat is a little Batman, instead of fighting crime, fighting these serious and debilitating diseases, Malaria, Dengue, Chikungunya, Zika, Yellow Fever, West Nile, Japanese Encephalitis...
Oh, and they reforest tropical forests, disperse seeds and fertilize as well - the Max Planck Institute in Radolfzell (with colleagues from Sweden and Ghana), have calculated the ecological/financial benefits of straw-coloured fruit bats in Africa. So, every night, these bats fly long distances to their feeding grounds, which means they disseminate the seeds of the fruits they consume. So, 150,000 animals disseminate more than 300,000 small seeds in a single night. This is sufficient to kickstart the regrowth of 800 hectares of forest -  the animals of one single bat colony...!

comments.body: Some day, when I become a 'Real Boy' I will read books. Not today, maybe not tomorrow, but some day. On that day, the 1st book that I will read will be 'Heather' aka 'Calluna vulgaris' which is a shrub found more often in fields than in forests. I had thought that the title of the book 'Heather' was attributed to a person named Heather, but I did a cursory search and found no reference to a first name Heather, so who is this Heather character? This is the mystery to me. Who or What Is Heather? I guess I will have to read it to find out.

Yes, cell service drops out in a few places but we are driving through the woods - exactly what I would expect to happen.

comments.name: Sinc MacRae
comments.body:
The challenge of finding a career that marries what one excels at with what one finds rewarding is a problem Plato discussed in The Republic more than 2000 years ago. Success in this does not turn on whether one embraces some gimmicky “zone of genius” expression. Indeed, framing the issue in this way fosters the same illusion of control that those who explain their good fortune by appealing to their alleged “genius” are guilty of. The simple truth is that we are all subject to the career lottery to one degree or another. Claiming that success in this lottery is determined by individual effort places the blame for failure and the praise for success at the feet of individual lottery ticket holders rather than the external social forces and dumb luck that largely determine such outcomes. 
 
Sure, we should work hard to intelligently develop and pursue our passions, but it is far better to work together to shape those external social forces to create general working conditions that are humane and dignified and in which the benefits of cooperation are shared more equitably so that one’s success in life does not turn so sharply on winning the career lottery along with the largely illusory zero-sum status gains that attend that.

comments.name: Steeben
comments.body:
“The Big Leap,” describes the intersection between one’s skills and passions.

This is completely wrong.  You have abilities and you have interests (not passions). They key is to discover your abilities and find way to pursue interests in vocations that the world needs (and can pay for).  Your abilities and interests then drive your skill development and hopefully you will eventually become very good at what you do.  It takes time.  Interests change.  Needs change.  Skill requirements change. It's called career management.

The problem with following your passions is that it leads one to believe that following them is an end in itself, with total disregard for whether that passion is marketable.  

Interests are broader and more applicable to a number of vocations; leave your passions for a hobby.

comments.name: Thomas Scheurich
comments.body:
I am sometimes considered "ingenious" by others and myself. It's pretty much always in strange and spiky ways that capitalism can make no use of. For others, there's no genius there, only steady application and team play. Or they don't like the idea of genius and profession lining up too often, for instance because they've never had a zone of genius for which credit and profits weren't instantly claimed by a superior in the hierarchy. Or they don't like to feel superior to their peers. 

Between all these groups, people like me and the others listed, this idea just doesn't work for most people. It's not a system solution to the potential job destruction. 

I do see the merit in it. It's absolutely right about what AI is showing no signs of doing. It's a way you can take responsibility for yourself in a nasty time. 

But there's one more pretty serious strike against it. People that are ingenious or insightful... That doesn't come from nowhere. It comes from a steady flow, which includes drudgerous task, easily automated tasks, routines that shape the cognitive innards (not unlike and often alongside the body). You don't become a great reporter without doing cub reporter research and tech editing. Etc. This idea is one piece of the picture... But just doesn't solve the problem, or anywhere close.

comments.name: Tom Debley
comments.body:
As this article points out, more and more voters are turning to AI for information about political candidates. That makes one habit worth sharing.

When I ask AI about any political issue—or any subject where accuracy matters—I begin my prompt with a simple instruction: "Using and citing only information from verifiable sources..." The response then typically includes hyperlinks to the original reporting, government documents, academic studies, or other primary sources.

Is it perfect? Certainly not. AI can still make mistakes or misinterpret evidence. But requiring verifiable sources gives me something invaluable: the ability to click through, read the original material, and judge the credibility of the source for myself. Sometimes I find the information persuasive; sometimes I reject it because the source isn't reliable or doesn't support the conclusion.

As AI becomes a common tool for voters, perhaps the most important skill won't be knowing how to ask questions—it will be learning how to ask for evidence. AI should be the beginning of our research, not the end of our thinking.

comments.body: One complaint I’ve heard repeatedly this summer - especially yesterday - is that Trump and ICE have imprisoned or deported all the reliable laborers on whom we Hill Country Texans have long depended for competent assistance in flood and disaster recovery. Our human labor force for cleanup and reconstruction was severely depleted because of Trump and ICE as our Hispanic neighbors became invisible out of fear in the last year-and-half. ICE conducts stops on our streets of our neighbors. No longer do Hispanic families shop at our many local thrift stores (I volunteer at a church thrift - Hispanic families that shopped in our store for decades have disappeared). A postal employee relative recounts how regulars on his route will no longer answer their door for mail delivery. Trump (and Abbott and Paxton) terrorized our Hispanic neighbors into hiding when we need their help desperately. We will remember this November.

comments.name: Partners
comments.body: My daughters - now in their forties - took preschool dance classes with Peggy Jean and CeCe - then a teenager. All the small businesses in their area suffered extensive damage - sports gear and cycling shops, television and video gear, our regional healthcare system’s urgent care location. After last year’s disaster, I’d returned to the joy of cycling our River Trail to grocery, yoga, church - leaving my car in the garage. Now I struggle to comprehend the stunning losses of friends whose homes near to creeks are flooded for the first time, neighbors on my street next to the river flooded for the second time in a year and 13 days, and the loss of our magnificent lifestyle. I just adopted a lab whose great joy was daily off-leash runs at the county dog park along the river - she’s frantic with unreleased energy in the last two days without access to the destroyed park. And my feral cat colony that I sustained for over three years along the creek bed meadow across the street - the cats survived but their meadow and all the trees, wildflowers were washed away. The feral cats are now in our street, challenging domesticated cats for territory, afraid of the human they once allowed to pet them as they fed on their limestone ledge overlooking the creek. Repeated flooding changes everything in our lives. Beauty is gone for now.
